question_text: A company wants to predict customer churn using structured tabular data with features such as account age, monthly spend, and number of support tickets. The team wants to use a SageMaker built-in algorithm that handles missing values natively and is well-suited for classification on tabular data. Which algorithm should the ML engineer use?
explanation: XGBoost is the most commonly tested SageMaker built-in algorithm for tabular classification and regression. It handles missing values natively without preprocessing, produces excellent results on structured data, and is the default choice when the exam describes tabular data with a classification or regression objective. Linear Learner is simpler and works for linear relationships but XGBoost outperforms it on complex tabular data. K-Means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm not a classification algorithm. Random Cut Forest is for anomaly detection not classification.

question_text: A retail company wants to add a product recommendation feature to its website. Customers should receive personalized recommendations based on their browsing and purchase history. question_text: A logistics company receives thousands of scanned shipping documents in PDF format daily. The documents contain structured tables with item descriptions, quantities, and prices as well as handwritten signature fields. The team needs to automatically extract this structured information into a database. Which AWS service is most appropriate?
explanation: Amazon Textract is correct because it extracts text, forms, and tables from scanned documents and PDFs — going beyond simple OCR to understand document structure. It can extract key-value pairs from forms and rows from tables. Amazon Rekognition analyzes images for visual content like objects, faces, and labels but does not extract structured document text. Amazon Comprehend performs NLP on plain text but does not handle document parsing or table extraction. Amazon Transcribe converts audio speech to text not document images.

question_text: A company operates 5000 retail stores and wants to forecast weekly demand for each product at each store location. The time series data shows strong seasonal patterns and correlations between related products. The team wants a SageMaker built-in algorithm that can model thousands of related time series simultaneously. Which algorithm is best suited?
explanation: DeepAR is correct for forecasting multiple related time series simultaneously. Unlike classical methods that model each series independently, DeepAR uses recurrent neural networks trained on all time series together, learning correlations between stores and products. This makes it ideal for large-scale retail forecasting. Linear Learner does not handle time series patterns. K-Means is unsupervised clustering not forecasting. XGBoost can be used for time series but requires manual feature engineering of lag variables and does not natively handle thousands of correlated series the way DeepAR does.

question_text: A cybersecurity team monitors network traffic logs and wants to automatically detect anomalous behavior that could indicate a security breach. The team has no labeled examples of malicious traffic. They want to assign an anomaly score to each network connection event. Which SageMaker built-in algorithm is designed for this use case?
explanation: Random Cut Forest (RCF) is the correct SageMaker built-in algorithm for anomaly detection. It assigns an anomaly score to each data point — higher scores indicate more anomalous behavior. Crucially it is unsupervised so it does not require labeled attack examples. XGBoost requires labeled data for classification. K-Means performs unsupervised clustering for grouping not anomaly scoring. Linear Learner is for regression and classification with labeled data not unsupervised anomaly detection.

question_text: A company has a high-dimensional customer dataset with 500 features per customer record. Many features are highly correlated. Before training a clustering model, the ML engineer wants to reduce dimensionality to remove redundant information and speed up training. Which SageMaker built-in algorithm should be applied first?
explanation: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is correct for dimensionality reduction. It transforms correlated features into uncorrelated principal components ordered by the amount of variance they explain. This reduces the 500 features to a smaller set of components that capture most of the variance, removing redundancy before clustering. XGBoost is a supervised algorithm not for dimensionality reduction. K-Means is the clustering step that would run after PCA not before. DeepAR is a time series forecasting algorithm not dimensionality reduction.

question_text: A company wants to build a generative AI chatbot that answers questions about their internal knowledge base of technical documentation. The foundation model should generate accurate responses grounded in the company's own documents rather than hallucinating information. Which Amazon Bedrock feature implements this architecture?
explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases implements Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by connecting a foundation model to a vector store containing the company's documents. When a question is asked, the system retrieves relevant document chunks and passes them as context to the foundation model, grounding responses in actual company documentation. Bedrock Guardrails controls content safety and filtering but does not connect the model to external knowledge. SageMaker JumpStart deploys pre-trained models but does not provide RAG architecture. Amazon Kendra is an enterprise search service that can be part of a RAG pipeline but Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the native Bedrock solution.

question_text: A company wants to segment one million customers into distinct behavioral groups for targeted marketing campaigns. question_text: A company has a proprietary dataset of 200000 labeled medical images for diagnosing skin conditions. The team wants to train an image classification model but does not want to build a deep learning architecture from scratch. They want to start from a pre-trained vision model and adapt it to their medical images. Which approach should the ML engineer use?
explanation: Transfer learning using SageMaker JumpStart is correct. JumpStart provides pre-trained image classification models (ResNet, EfficientNet, ViT) that can be fine-tuned on custom datasets using the built-in fine-tuning functionality. The team gets the benefit of features learned from millions of images pre-training while specializing the model on their 200000 medical images. Training from scratch requires far more data and compute. Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels also allows custom image classification without ML expertise but JumpStart provides more control for a team comfortable with SageMaker.
option_text: Train the SageMaker Image Classification algorithm from scratch on the 200000 images

question_text: A company wants to build a generative AI application that generates product descriptions for their catalog. The application must never produce content about competitor products, must not output text containing customer names or account numbers, and must detect and block attempts by users to bypass these restrictions through prompt injection attacks. Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides document grounding for RAG but does not provide content filtering. Bedrock Agents orchestrates multi-step AI workflows but does not provide content safety policies. SageMaker Clarify detects model bias not generative AI content safety.
option_text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with document filtering

question_text: A manufacturing company monitors 200 industrial sensors measuring temperature, pressure, and vibration. Each sensor produces readings every second. The team wants to detect when a combination of sensor readings suggests impending equipment failure before it occurs — a pattern that is not present in any labeled historical data since the equipment has rarely failed. Which SageMaker approach is best suited?
explanation: Random Cut Forest is correct for this use case because it is an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm — no labeled failure examples are required. It assigns anomaly scores to multivariate sensor readings in real time, flagging unusual combinations of temperature, pressure, and vibration patterns that deviate from normal operating conditions. XGBoost requires labeled failure/no-failure examples. DeepAR forecasts future values of time series but does not flag anomalies across correlated multivariate sensors. K-Means clusters data but does not provide an anomaly score for individual readings.
option_text: SageMaker XGBoost binary classifier trained on labeled sensor failure events

question_text: A company is building an AI assistant for enterprise employees that answers questions by searching internal SharePoint documents, Confluence wikis, and Jira tickets. Responses must be grounded in the actual document content — the assistant must not hallucinate answers that are not in the source documents. Which Amazon Bedrock architecture implements this correctly?
explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases implements the RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pattern. Source documents (SharePoint, Confluence, Jira) are ingested, chunked, and stored as vector embeddings in a vector store. When a question is asked, relevant chunks are retrieved and passed as context to the foundation model which generates a response grounded in the actual document content. Bedrock Guardrails prevents harmful content but does not connect the model to documents. Bedrock Agents orchestrates tool use but alone does not implement document-grounded responses. SageMaker JumpStart fine-tunes models which would memorize training data not dynamically retrieve current document content.
option_text: Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to block any responses not found in company documents
